cards.q: What is IPv4 multicast and what models does it support?
cards.a: It delivers traffic to a group of interested receivers: the source sends to one multicast group and the network replicates traffic only where needed, using Class D 224.0.0.0/4. Models are one-to-many, many-to-many, and source-specific multicast (SSM) with (S,G); uses include IPTV, streaming, financial feeds, and OSPF/EIGRP/RIPv2.

cards.q: What is the IPv4 multicast address range and what do the addresses identify?
cards.a: 224.0.0.0/4, spanning 224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255 and historically called Class D; multicast addresses identify groups, not individual interfaces, and there is no host/network portion within a multicast address.

cards.q: What are the important IPv4 multicast sub-ranges?
cards.a: 224.0.0.0/24 is link-local multicast; 224.0.1.0–238.255.255.255 is globally scoped/administratively assignable space; and 239.0.0.0/8 is administratively scoped multicast for private/organizational domains.

cards.q: What are the well-known link-local multicast addresses?
cards.a: 224.0.0.1 all IPv4 hosts, 224.0.0.2 all multicast routers, 224.0.0.5 OSPF routers, 224.0.0.6 OSPF DRs/BDRs, 224.0.0.9 RIPv2, 224.0.0.10 EIGRP, and 224.0.0.22 IGMPv3.

cards.q: Do routers forward traffic destined for 224.0.0.0/24?
cards.a: No; 224.0.0.0/24 is link-local multicast and is not forwarded by multicast routers, which is why multicast control traffic such as OSPF hellos stays on the local network segment.

cards.q: What is the role of IGMP in IPv4 multicast?
cards.a: IGMP is a Layer 3 host/router membership protocol used between IPv4 hosts and their directly connected multicast routers, letting a host join a group (I want to receive 239.1.1.1); IGMP answers which hosts want the group, not how to route multicast.

cards.q: What is PIM and what are its modes?
cards.a: PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) is the multicast routing protocol that builds distribution trees; PIM-DM floods traffic then prunes branches without receivers, PIM-SM assumes sparse receivers and commonly uses a Rendezvous Point, and PIM-SSM uses (S,G) source/group subscriptions.

cards.q: What is (S,G) notation in source-specific multicast?
cards.a: (S,G) is the source-plus-group pair, e.g. (192.168.10.10, 232.1.1.1); SSM uses the range 232.0.0.0/8 and does not require a Rendezvous Point.

cards.q: Is the Rendezvous Point associated with SSM?
cards.a: No; the RP is associated with PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), not with PIM-SSM. SSM uses source-specific (S,G) subscriptions and requires no RP.

cards.q: How is IPv4 multicast mapped to an Ethernet multicast MAC address?
cards.a: The Ethernet multicast MAC range is 01:00:5E:00:00:00 through 01:00:5E:7F:FF:FF (format 01:00:5E:0x:xx:xx); of the 28 IPv4 multicast bits, only 23 are mapped to the MAC, so 5 bits are lost.

cards.q: How many IPv4 multicast addresses can map to the same Ethernet multicast MAC and why?
cards.a: 32 (2^5), because the 28-bit IPv4 multicast portion maps into only 23 bits of the Ethernet MAC, discarding 5 bits; this many-to-one mapping cannot uniquely identify every IPv4 multicast group.

cards.q: Does a multicast IP-to-MAC collision mean the IP groups are identical?
cards.a: No; the 32-to-1 MAC mapping is simply a normal limitation of the Layer 2 mapping, and the distinct IP multicast groups are not made identical by sharing a MAC address.

cards.q: What is IGMP snooping and where does it operate?
cards.a: It is a Layer 2 switch feature that listens to IGMP messages and builds forwarding state, sending multicast only toward ports with interested receivers instead of flooding the VLAN; IGMP itself remains a Layer 3 host/router membership protocol.

Unicast is one-to-one to a specific host (HTTP, SSH); broadcast is one-to-all within the broadcast domain (ARP, DHCP Discover) and normally not routed; multicast is one-to-many or many-to-many to interested group members (IPTV, streaming, routing protocols), is routed, and replicates only where needed.

cards.q: How does TTL affect link-local multicast control traffic?
cards.a: Many local multicast control protocols use TTL = 1 to stay on the local segment; the key ENCOR rule is that traffic to 224.0.0.0/24 is link-local multicast and is not forwarded by multicast routers even with a higher TTL.

cards.q: How do you configure and verify multicast on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: Enable ip multicast-routing globally; configure ip pim sparse-mode on the relevant Layer 3 interfaces; set ip igmp version 3 on interfaces when IGMPv3/SSM support is needed; verify with show ip mroute (multicast routing table) and show ip igmp groups.

cards.q: Can you subnet multicast addresses like normal unicast addresses?
cards.a: No; 224.0.0.0/4 defines the multicast space and multicast addresses identify groups, so there is no host/network split and you do not calculate normal unicast host counts for Class D.

cards.q: Is multicast the same as broadcast?
cards.a: No; broadcast delivers to all hosts in the broadcast domain, while multicast delivers only to interested group members, making it specifically designed for group-based delivery.

Range 224.0.0.0/4 (Class D); link-local 224.0.0.0/24; admin-scoped 239.0.0.0/8; SSM 232.0.0.0/8; Ethernet multicast MAC 01:00:5E:0x:xx:xx; 28 IPv4 bits mapped to 23 MAC bits (5 lost, 32-to-1 collision); membership via IGMP (v1/v2/v3), routing via PIM; PIM-SM uses an RP, PIM-SSM uses (S,G) with no RP; switch optimization via IGMP snooping.
